name: Skin whitening/bleaching

card.summary: Lightening skin tone with topical agents, supplements or injections, discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to raise appearance scores; the practice is long-established worldwide and carries well-documented risks.
card.aka: Skin lightening, skin bleaching, depigmentation, whitemaxxing
card.note: Regulators and reviews document harms from mercury, steroid and hydroquinone products and from intravenous glutathione.

quick.overview:
Skin whitening means using chemical agents to reduce melanin and lighten skin tone. It predates the internet by centuries and is practiced in many regions for cultural, social and medical reasons. On looksmaxxing forums it appears as a method some posters say improves their ratings.

Research exists on individual agents such as kojic acid, hydroquinone and glutathione, mostly in the context of pigmentation disorders. Dermatology reviews also describe cosmetic lightening as a public health and sociocultural issue.
quick.mechanism: Most lightening agents work by inhibiting tyrosinase, the key enzyme in melanin production. Others block the transfer of melanin to skin cells or destroy melanocytes. Glutathione is reported to inhibit tyrosinase and shift melanin production from eumelanin toward phaeomelanin.
quick.risks: Reported harms include mercury toxicity from contaminated products, skin thinning and other effects from long-term steroid creams, ochronosis and contact dermatitis from hydroquinone, and serious reactions from intravenous glutathione. Many products are restricted or banned in several countries, and sun sensitivity rises in users.

lead: Skin whitening, also called skin lightening or bleaching, is the use of chemical substances to lighten skin color or even out tone by reducing melanin. Recorded practices date back more than two thousand years, and use is widespread across Africa, Asia and elsewhere. [1]

A 2022 dermatology review describes cosmetic skin lightening as a growing public health problem among communities of color, with well-documented adverse health effects alongside social and cultural drivers. [2] Reviews of the agents themselves, such as glutathione, describe a gap between popular use and evidence of efficacy and safety. [3][4]

On looksmax.org the topic is discussed by some users as a looksmaxxing tactic, often alongside ethnicity and the PSL rating scale; posts include claims that lightening adds to a rating and recommendations of particular products. [5]

Hydroquinone, tretinoin and corticosteroids banned in cosmetics [1]

paras: Agents range from topical creams to oral supplements and injections. Wikipedia lists hydroquinone, kojic acid, alpha hydroxy acids, tretinoin, corticosteroids such as clobetasol, glutathione and inorganic mercury among the substances used, and notes that some are effective while others are toxic or of questionable safety. [1] A medicinal chemistry review describes tyrosinase inhibitors as the main route of drug development. [6]

Wikipedia traces lightening practices to antiquity in Egypt, Greece and East Asia, and to lead-based preparations in Elizabethan Europe, with commercial products marketed in the 19th and 20th centuries United States. [1] It reports usage figures from a 2013 source of 77% of Nigerian women, 52% of Senegalese women and 25% of Malian women, and describes motivations including associations of lighter skin with beauty, status and marriage prospects, as well as treatment of pigmentation conditions. [1]

Critics cited in the same article say the practice reinforces colorism, while the dermatology review frames it as a practice with sociocultural implications that clinicians should discuss sensitively with patients. [1][2]

A 2016 review of glutathione as a skin-lightening agent found a dichotomy between popularity and evidence, noting that no evidence supports the efficacy of intravenous injections and that adverse effects led the Philippine FDA to issue warnings. [3] A 2025 narrative review reported significant but variable melanin reductions with oral glutathione and good-level reductions with topical forms of varying sustainability, while describing intravenous use as associated with serious safety concerns such as anaphylaxis and hepatotoxicity and calling for large, rigorous trials. [4]
Wikipedia states that the effectiveness of glutathione was unclear as of 2019, and that kojic acid has been reported as effective in some studies. [1]

Clinical evidence consists mainly of reviews and small trials of individual agents, chiefly glutathione, examined for melasma and other pigmentation uses or skin tone. [3][4] No studies found that test whether lightening skin changes attractiveness ratings or dating outcomes, the claim made in forum threads. [5]

Wikipedia lists mercury toxicity (neurological and kidney damage), hydroquinone-linked ochronosis, cataracts and dermatitis, and long-term corticosteroid effects such as skin atrophy and glaucoma, along with greater sun sensitivity and infection risk. [1] It also reports that many such products are illegal in various countries yet remain on sale, with weak enforcement. [1]
Reviews also describe serious adverse events associated with intravenous glutathione. [3][4]

A looksmax.org thread on the subject opens by saying lightening adds half a point to a full point of PSL and lists groups the poster thinks it applies to, products such as kojic acid soap and video channels; replies dispute whether lighter skin is desirable. [5] No published study has evaluated the PSL scale or such claimed gains.

timeline.event: Earliest recorded skin-lightening practices in several civilizations. [1]
South Africa begins regulating mercury and hydroquinone products. [1]
Review finds no evidence for intravenous glutathione efficacy and notes Philippine FDA warnings. [3]
Narrative review calls for rigorous trials of glutathione for lightening. [4]

lore.intro: Skin lightening is discussed on looksmax.org as a method to change one's rating or ethnic appearance, with debate over whether lighter skin is more attractive. [5]

claims.claim: Lightening skin adds about 0.5 to 1 PSL.
claims.believers: A forum poster states that it adds this much and lists who it is suitable for. [5]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined whether skin tone changes ratings on the PSL scale, which is an informal community scale. [1]

claims.claim: Kojic acid, arbutin and hydroquinone products can lighten skin.
claims.believers: Posters recommend kojic acid soap and other products. [5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports kojic acid as effective in some studies and hydroquinone as a common melanin-reducing agent, while noting the EU ban on hydroquinone in cosmetics and documented harms. [1][6]

claims.believers: Forum posts link to channels documenting a glutathione journey. [5]
claims.experts: Reviews report variable reductions in melanin with oral use and no evidence of efficacy for intravenous use, with serious safety concerns including anaphylaxis and liver toxicity. [3][4]

claims.claim: Mercury or steroid-containing creams lighten skin.
claims.believers: The forum thread cited here focuses on other products and does not discuss mercury or steroid creams.
claims.experts: Wikipedia documents mercury toxicity and steroid-related effects and says such products are illegal in many places. [1]
